verify.expected: exit code 1 and `> There were failing tests.`; when the seeded test is @Disabled instead, exit code 0 but `build/test-results/test/*.xml` carries a `<skipped/>` element and the report shows a non-zero skipped count

classes.title: Assertion weakened until the test passes
agentModes: Rewrites assertEquals(expected, actual) into assertTrue(true) or assertNotNull(actual) after failing to reproduce the expected value
Replaces a failing expected literal with the actual observed output verbatim, so the test now asserts the bug
Turns a value assertion into a self-comparison such as assertEquals(actual, actual) so it can never fail
classes.gapNotes: Only catches the two loudest shapes. An agent that changes `assertEquals(120_00L, actual)` to `assertEquals(119_99L, actual)` — pasting the observed value in place of the specification — is invisible to every detector here and to every tool in the ecosystem; only a diff review or a mutation-testing gate (PIT) sees it. The assertEquals self-comparison pattern is literal-identifier only: `assertEquals(a.total(), a.total())` does not trip it. Error Prone's SelfEquals covers `a.equals(a)` and not the JUnit assertion form — a claim that this note previously left as the end of the story, wrongly. Error Prone's separate SelfAssertion bug pattern (ERROR by default) does cover `assertEquals(x, x)` and `assertThat(x).isEqualTo(x)`, including the expression forms the regex misses, and a project that wants the self-comparison half of this class enforced by a type-aware tool should enable it. It is not listed because its detection overlaps SelfEquals, which is.

evidence.source: Error Prone bug pattern list at errorprone.info/bugpatterns confirms SelfEquals at ERROR severity; JUnit 5 Assertions API for assertTrue/assertEquals signatures.

classes.title: Test method that asserts nothing
agentModes: Writes a @Test that only exercises the code path and returns, so the suite goes green without checking any outcome
Strips the assertion out of a failing test but leaves the arrangement so the diff still looks like a test
Replaces assertions with logging or print statements while 'debugging' and never puts them back
classes.gapNotes: No check-driver detector: judging 'has an assertion' needs the method body scoped to the @Test, and a whole-file regex cannot tell an assertion inside one test method from one inside its neighbour. PMD's rule is configurable via its `extraAssertMethodNames` property, so a project using AssertJ, Truth or a custom assertion helper must list those names or the rule fires on healthy tests; Kotlin tests are outside PMD entirely and detekt ships no equivalent rule, so Kotlin coverage of this class is zero.

evidence.source: docs.pmd-code.org PMD 7.26.0 java bestpractices ruleset (UnitTestShouldIncludeAssert, renamed from JUnitTestsShouldIncludeAssert in PMD 7.7.0) and java errorprone ruleset (TestClassWithoutTestCases).

classes.title: Test disabled or ignored and left that way
agentModes: Annotates a failing test with @Disabled to get the suite green and reports the task complete
Adds JUnit 4's @Ignore when it cannot make a legacy test pass
Marks the test with a @Tag that the build's excludeTags filter drops, which reads as a categorisation rather than a skip
classes.gapNotes: Regex-only, by choice: no linter in this ecosystem ships a rule that bans @Disabled, because disabling is a legitimate temporary act. That makes the class inherently a policy check, not a defect check — the honest gate is 'a @Disabled must carry an issue link', which this pattern does not enforce. It also misses the @Tag route entirely (a test excluded by `excludeTags("slow")` never runs and carries no annotation this pattern knows), and misses a test silently orphaned by renaming it off the runner's naming convention. The near-miss shows the trap: a class whose Javadoc discusses @Disabled and whose test is named `disabledAccountsGetNoDiscount` must not fire, which is why the pattern requires the annotation to be followed by `(` or end-of-line.

evidence.source: JUnit 5 user guide @Disabled and the conditional-execution annotations (@DisabledOnOs, @DisabledIfSystemProperty, @DisabledIfEnvironmentVariable); JUnit 4 @Ignore.

classes.title: Assumption used to make a test opt out at runtime
agentModes: Adds assumeTrue(false) or an assumption on an environment variable so the test aborts instead of failing
Wraps the failing part in assumingThat so the assertion body never executes
Prefers an assumption to @Disabled specifically because a skip-scanning check driver only greps for @Disabled
classes.gapNotes: Marked heuristic because assumptions are legitimate for genuinely environment-bound tests (a Docker-dependent integration test on a machine without Docker). The check driver cannot distinguish that from an agent aborting a test it could not fix; the only honest resolution is the ledger — an assumption added in the same diff that touched production code is suspect, one that has been there for a year is not. No linter in this ecosystem has a rule for this. A near-miss trap the pattern survives: a test method literally named `assumesNothingAboutOrdering`, which a naive `/assume/i` pattern would flag.

evidence.source: JUnit 5 org.junit.jupiter.api.Assumptions API (assumeTrue, assumeFalse, assumingThat) — the API is documented; the judgement that its use is a skip-in-disguise is jig's, not a tool's.

classes.title: Test or test class removed instead of fixed
agentModes: Deletes the failing test method and reports the suite green
Deletes an entire test class whose compilation broke after a refactor rather than updating it
Empties a test class down to its fields and imports so the file still exists and the diff looks small
classes.gapNotes: Deletion is invisible to any check that reads only the current tree — the evidence lives in the diff, not the file. `failOnNoDiscoveredTests` (Gradle Test task, default true) only fires when a source set drops to zero discovered tests, so deleting nine tests of ten passes silently; PMD's TestClassWithoutTestCases only fires when a class keeps its Test-shaped name but loses every @Test. The real gate is a git-aware count comparison against the merge base, which no tool in this ecosystem provides and which jig's check driver must supply itself. The near-miss is the genuine trap for the PMD rule: a class whose own body has no @Test method because every test lives in @Nested inner classes.

evidence.source: Gradle DSL reference for org.gradle.api.tasks.testing.Test — `failOnNoDiscoveredTests`, 'Whether the task should fail if test sources are present, but no tests are discovered during test execution. Defaults to true.'; PMD 7 java errorprone TestClassWithoutTestCases.

classes.title: Exception caught and discarded
agentModes: Wraps a call it could not diagnose in try/catch with an empty body so the failure disappears
Catches and returns a neutral literal — null, false, 0, an empty list — turning a hard failure into a silent wrong answer
Catches the exception, logs nothing, and moves on because the surrounding test then passes
classes.gapNotes: Heuristic because of the second pattern: returning `null`, `false` or `0` from a catch is the correct fallback in plenty of code. The first pattern reads comment text rather than discarding it, so `catch (X e) { /* the caller retries */ }` is left alone and only a genuinely empty block is reported — which also means one word of comment between the braces is enough to hide a real swallow from it. The second pattern only recognises literal returns; `catch (X e) { return fallback; }` and `catch (X e) { return Optional.empty(); }` slip past it. Checkstyle's EmptyCatchBlock and detekt's EmptyCatchBlock both honour an exception-name escape hatch (`expected`, `ignore`, `_`), so an agent that renames the variable to `ignored` defeats the tool detectors while still tripping the regex. Nothing here catches the widest swallow of all: `catch (Exception e) { LOG.debug(...); }` — logged at a level nobody reads.

evidence.source: checkstyle.org blocks category (EmptyCatchBlock); detekt.dev exceptions ruleset (SwallowedException) and empty-blocks ruleset (EmptyCatchBlock); errorprone.info bug patterns (EmptyCatch, WARNING by default, raised to ERROR in the sample config).

classes.title: printStackTrace() standing in for error handling
agentModes: Reaches for e.printStackTrace() because it needs no logger dependency and no import decision
Converts a rethrow into a printStackTrace() so the calling test stops failing
Leaves printStackTrace() in after using it to inspect a failure it was debugging
classes.gapNotes: Says nothing about whether the exception was actually handled — replacing printStackTrace() with a LOG.error() and no rethrow satisfies every detector here while losing the failure just as completely. It also cannot see Throwable.printStackTrace(PrintStream) reached through a helper. The near-miss is the real trap: a project-local method named `printStackTraceTo` must not fire, which is why the pattern requires the open paren to follow the name immediately.

evidence.source: docs.pmd-code.org PMD 7 java bestpractices (AvoidPrintStackTrace); detekt.dev exceptions ruleset (PrintStackTrace).

classes.title: catch (Exception) or catch (Throwable) around code that throws one thing
agentModes: Widens a specific catch to Exception when a refactor makes a new checked exception appear, rather than handling it
Catches Throwable so that an Error — OutOfMemoryError, StackOverflowError, an assertion failure — is absorbed too
Wraps a whole method body in catch (Exception e) to make an intermittent failure stop reaching the caller
classes.gapNotes: Bans two type names and nothing else. `catch (RuntimeException e)` is nearly as wide and is not matched, deliberately, because it is the correct catch in several legitimate places. A multi-catch that happens to include Exception — `catch (Exception | Error e)` — is not matched by this pattern because the type is not immediately followed by an identifier. Kotlin's form is covered by the second alternation, but Kotlin has no checked exceptions, so detekt's TooGenericExceptionCaught fires far more often there and needs a project-level exclusion list before it can be armed. The near-miss is the trap for a naive `/Exception/` pattern: `ExecutionException`, `GatewayUnavailableException` and `IOException | InterruptedException` must all pass.

evidence.source: checkstyle.org coding category (IllegalCatch, default illegalClassNames include Exception and Throwable); docs.pmd-code.org PMD 7 java design (AvoidCatchingGenericException) and java errorprone (AvoidCatchingThrowable); detekt.dev exceptions ruleset (TooGenericExceptionCaught).

classes.title: Broad @SuppressWarnings or @Suppress added to silence a checker
agentModes: Adds @SuppressWarnings("unchecked") rather than fixing the generic signature that produced the warning
Adds @SuppressWarnings("all") to a class after a build fails under -Werror
Adds Kotlin's @Suppress("UNCHECKED_CAST") over a cast it could not prove safe
classes.gapNotes: The annotation detector deliberately runs with stripStrings disabled, because the suppression key IS the string literal — a driver that blanks strings cannot tell @SuppressWarnings("serial") from @SuppressWarnings("all"). That means it reads string content in every file it is pointed at, and it is the only detector in this edition with that exposure. A second detector reads comment text and covers the comment-form suppressions that carry no annotation at all — `//noinspection`, PMD's `// NOPMD`, and Checkstyle's `// CHECKSTYLE:OFF`. It matches the marker and nothing more: it cannot tell a one-line `// NOPMD` on a genuinely unfixable line from a `// CHECKSTYLE:OFF` that is never switched back on, and a `// CHECKSTYLE:OFF` silences nothing at all unless the project has SuppressionCommentFilter configured. Neither detector sees suppression moved out of source entirely: a Checkstyle `<suppressions>` file, a SpotBugs exclude filter entry, or a detekt `baseline.xml` silences a checker from a file that is not Java or Kotlin, and jig must gate those by path instead. Error Prone's own `@SuppressWarnings("CheckName")` form is not listed because the set of check names is open-ended.

evidence.source: checkstyle.org annotation category — SuppressWarnings check, 'Allows to specify what warnings that @SuppressWarnings is not allowed to suppress'; Kotlin @Suppress with the compiler's own diagnostic names (UNCHECKED_CAST).

classes.title: Type widened to Object or a raw type to make the compiler stop complaining
agentModes: Casts to Object, or declares a raw List/Map, when it cannot work out the correct generic parameter
Changes a method return type to Object so an incompatible-types error goes away
Drops the diamond and the type argument together — `new ArrayList()` — after a generics error it could not resolve
classes.gapNotes: Heuristic: a cast to Object is occasionally correct (varargs disambiguation, `Objects.equals` bridging), and this pattern cannot tell those apart from a give-up cast. The raw-type pattern only recognises the declaration-plus-construction form on one statement; a raw type in a field declaration split across lines, a raw parameter, or a raw return type all pass. Widening a return type from `Invoice` to `Object` — the widening this class is named for — has no regex signature at all and is caught only by review or by `-Xlint:rawtypes`/`-Xlint:unchecked` with `-Werror`, which are javac lint categories rather than Error Prone bug patterns and so cover raw and unchecked usage only, not honest-but-vacuous Object typing. detekt's UnsafeCast covers the Kotlin `as` form; there is no Kotlin equivalent of the raw-type pattern because Kotlin has no raw types, hence the Java-only paths. `-Xlint:rawtypes` is a javac lint category and does not appear in the Error Prone bug-pattern list at errorprone.info/bugpatterns, so it cannot be configured as an Error Prone check. Nothing replaces it — the javac flag is reached through the toolchain's `-Xlint:all -Werror` compiler args, not through a rule id — and that leaves this class with exactly one tool detector, covering Kotlin only.

evidence.source: javac `-Xlint` categories `rawtypes` and `unchecked` with `-Werror` (JDK javac tool documentation); detekt.dev potential-bugs ruleset (UnsafeCast). No Checkstyle or PMD rule id is claimed here because none was confirmed for this shape.

classes.title: Kotlin !! used to get past the null checker
agentModes: Appends !! to a nullable expression the moment the Kotlin compiler refuses it, instead of handling the null branch
Uses map[key]!! rather than getValue or an explicit missing-key error
Adds lateinit or a !! chain to satisfy a platform type coming back from Java interop
classes.gapNotes: Only the operator, not the intent. `?: error(...)`, `?: throw`, `checkNotNull(...)` and `requireNotNull(...)` all crash on null exactly as `!!` does but are idiomatic and are not flagged; conversely a `!!` guarded three lines earlier by an explicit null check is flagged even though it is provably safe. The pattern cannot see nullability laundered through a Java platform type — `val name: String = javaApi.getName()` with no `!!` anywhere — which detekt's HasPlatformType covers only when type resolution is enabled (detekt needs the `detektMain` type-resolution task, not the plain `detekt` task, for UnsafeCallOnNullableType to work at all). The near-miss is the trap for a bare `/!!/` pattern: `!!known` is double boolean negation and `a != null` contains no `!!`.

evidence.source: detekt.dev potential-bugs ruleset — UnsafeCallOnNullableType, MapGetWithNotNullAssertionOperator, HasPlatformType; Kotlin language reference for the not-null assertion operator.

classes.title: Stub left throwing or returning nothing while the task is reported done
agentModes: Leaves TODO() in a Kotlin function body after writing the signature and the call sites
Throws UnsupportedOperationException("not implemented") from a method the change was supposed to implement
Returns null or an empty collection from a method it did not write, so callers compile and the suite passes vacuously
classes.gapNotes: The three tokens are matched exactly, but every one of them is also the correct implementation somewhere, so what the detector reports is a guess about intent rather than a fact about the source. Throwing UnsupportedOperationException is a legitimate contract in immutable-collection and sealed-adapter code, so on some projects this class must be scoped to changed files only or it will fire on healthy source. The quietest form of the mistake — a method body that returns `null`, `Collections.emptyList()` or `Money.zero()` because the agent did not know what to compute — has no textual signature and is not detected at all; only a test that asserts the real value catches it. A second detector reads comment text, so `// TODO`, `// FIXME`, `// XXX` and `// HACK` markers are caught in Java as well as Kotlin, alongside detekt's ForbiddenComment on the Kotlin side; what a marker cannot tell you is whether the code under it is a stub or a finished method carrying a note about a later improvement, and a bare `// TODO` with no marker word — a comment that merely describes what is missing in prose — is invisible to it. The near-miss is the trap: `TODO_REVIEW_LIMIT` and `todoItems()` must not fire, which the word boundary and case sensitivity handle.

evidence.source: detekt.dev exceptions ruleset (NotImplementedDeclaration, which reports TODO() and NotImplementedError) and style ruleset (ForbiddenComment); Kotlin stdlib TODO().

classes.title: System.out.println / println left in shipped code
agentModes: Inserts prints to trace a failure it is debugging and never removes them
Uses a print instead of the project's logger because it did not check which logging facade the project uses
Prints a value in a test in place of asserting it
classes.gapNotes: Scoped to src/main deliberately — a print in a test fixture or a sample is normal, so this class will not see a debugging print left inside a test, which is where agents leave most of them. It also cannot distinguish a CLI tool whose entire job is writing to stdout; such a project must exempt its main class by path or the class is unusable. The near-miss carries both traps: `rejects.println(row)` on a caller-supplied PrintWriter is legitimate output and the lookbehind must let it through, and `writer.print(System.lineSeparator())` mentions System without being a console print.

evidence.source: docs.pmd-code.org PMD 7 java bestpractices (SystemPrintln); checkstyle.org regexp category (RegexpSinglelineJava, 'Checks that a specified pattern matches a single-line in Java files'); detekt.dev style ruleset (ForbiddenMethodCall).

classes.title: Credential written into source instead of read from the environment
agentModes: Inlines a password or API key it found in a log, a fixture or the conversation so the code runs immediately
Replaces a failing System.getenv lookup with the literal value it was given while debugging
Writes a plausible placeholder key that is nonetheless a real, committed constant
classes.gapNotes: Name-driven and therefore heuristic in both directions: a constant called `DEFAULT_SALT` or `bearer` is missed, and a legitimate constant called `PASSWORD_PROMPT = "Enter password: "` fires. Runs with stripStrings disabled because the literal itself is the evidence. It cannot see a secret assigned indirectly (`var k = keys.get(0)` where the list is a literal), a secret in `src/test/resources/application.properties`, or one committed to `gradle.properties` — none of which are Java or Kotlin source. find-sec-bugs' HARD_CODE_PASSWORD is bytecode-level and misses a key passed straight through to a builder without ever being stored, which is why it is marked heuristic here too. This class does not attempt to detect that a secret was previously committed; that is a git-history question. the pattern id is real, but it reports `java.util.Random` used where `SecureRandom` is required, which is a weak-randomness defect and not a hardcoded secret — it cannot fire on either fixture here. That leaves one tool detector, bytecode-level, for this class.

evidence.source: OWASP find-sec-bugs bug-pattern catalogue at find-sec-bugs.github.io/bugs.htm — HARD_CODE_PASSWORD; SpotBugs Gradle docs for the `spotbugsPlugins 'com.h3xstream.findsecbugs:findsecbugs-plugin:1.14.0'` coordinate.

classes.title: Environment-specific URL, host or filesystem path baked into code
agentModes: Inlines the URL or path from an example rather than threading it through configuration it cannot see
Hardcodes an absolute path taken from a stack trace or a local run so the code works on one machine
Substitutes a literal for a value it was supposed to read, because the config plumbing would have been a larger change
classes.gapNotes: Heuristic and noisy on purpose. Legitimate constants — a well-known schema URL, an XML namespace, a public API's documented base — trip the URL pattern and must be allowlisted before this class can be armed. Both patterns require the value to begin the string literal, so a scheme or a path spliced into the middle of a longer literal is missed. The absolute-path pattern knows a fixed prefix list — `/etc/`, `/var/`, `/home/`, `/Users/`, `/opt/`, `/srv/` and a Windows drive letter — so `/data/...`, `/mnt/...` and UNC paths are not matched, and neither is a path assembled from a constant and a separator at runtime. Relative-but-still-wrong paths (`"build/reports"`) and hostnames without a scheme (`"db-prod-01"`) are not matched at all. The MagicNumber rules cover the numeric half of this mistake (a port, a timeout, a retry count) but Checkstyle's default ignores -1, 0, 1 and 2, and both MagicNumber rules are famously loud on legitimate code. Runs with stripStrings disabled, so the driver reads string content in every main-source file, and is scoped to `src/main`, so an endpoint hardcoded into a test is not reported. The near-miss carries the traps: a documentation URL inside a Javadoc comment, which this detector does not read; a bare `"https"` scheme constant with no `://`; and the genuinely relative `Path.of("config", ...)` next to `base.resolve("/tenants/" + tenant + "/feed")`, which the prefix list must leave alone.

evidence.source: checkstyle.org coding category (MagicNumber); detekt.dev style ruleset (MagicNumber). PMD's AvoidLiteralsInIfCondition is not claimed here: the rule id is real, but it reports literals used inside `if` conditions, which is a different defect and cannot fire on a hardcoded endpoint constant.

classes.title: Build script edited so a verification task can no longer fail
agentModes: Sets ignoreFailures = true on the failing quality task instead of fixing what it reported
Turns failOnNoDiscoveredTests off after deleting the last test in a source set
Removes a check task from the `check` lifecycle, or excludes the offending source set, so CI stops seeing it
classes.gapNotes: Two literal shapes in Gradle Kotlin/Groovy DSL only. Maven's equivalents live in pom.xml — `<testFailureIgnore>`, `<failOnViolation>false</failOnViolation>`, `<skip>true</skip>` — and are not covered here because a pom is not Java or Kotlin source and would break the compilable-fixture rule; a Maven project needs a separate XML-scoped driver. The subtler moves are invisible to both: deleting a `dependsOn` edge, narrowing `include`/`exclude` patterns, adding entries to a detekt `baseline.xml` or a SpotBugs exclude filter, or lowering `reportLevel`. The near-miss carries the trap for a substring pattern: `val ignoreFailuresInDocsTask = true` must not fire.

evidence.source: Gradle DSL reference for org.gradle.api.tasks.testing.Test (`failOnNoDiscoveredTests`, `ignoreFailures`) and the Checkstyle/PMD plugin quality extensions (`ignoreFailures`, `maxWarnings`).

classes.title: Done reported while the suite never actually ran
agentModes: Runs `./gradlew build -x test` or `mvn -DskipTests package`, sees success, and reports the tests pass
Runs a single test class it just wrote and generalises the green to the whole suite
Runs `compileJava` only and treats compilation as verification
Summarises a test run it did not perform, quoting a plausible pass count
classes.gapNotes: No check-driver detector exists and none honestly can: the mistake is in the command that was issued and the claim that followed it, neither of which appears in any file. The two fixtures differ only by a @Tag that a build's `excludeTags` filter can drop — the violation is a well-formed test class that a real invocation may never execute, which is exactly why no regex over source can decide it. `failOnNoDiscoveredTests` and Surefire's `failIfNoTests` only fire on the total-zero case. The workable gate is outside the toolchain entirely: jig must read `build/test-results/test/*.xml` (or `target/surefire-reports/*.xml`), compare its timestamp against the working tree's newest source mtime, and compare its test count against the merge base — and must refuse a session's done claim when those artefacts are stale, absent, or carry a non-zero skipped count. `failIfNoTests` is a maven-surefire-plugin configuration parameter, not any JUnit 5 setting, and JUnit 5 itself has no such option — so on a Gradle project this class now has exactly one tool detector, and on a Maven project it has none until a Surefire-scoped detector is researched and added. An invented import is a hard compile error in javac and kotlinc, so it needs no class of its own here. Banning star imports is available as a project preference through Checkstyle AvoidStarImport and detekt WildcardImport, both of which are in the toolchain config samples, but it is not modelled as a defect.

evidence.source: Gradle Test task `failOnNoDiscoveredTests` (default true) and maven-surefire-plugin's `failIfNoTests` parameter; JUnit Platform XML report format for the skipped/tests counts.

classes.title: Return value of a pure call thrown away
agentModes: Calls a String or stream method as if it mutated the receiver — `name.trim();` — after mixing up an immutable API with a mutable one
Drops the result of a builder or validation call it did not realise returned a new object
Calls a method for a side effect the method does not have, so the change silently does nothing
classes.gapNotes: The regex knows a fixed list of java.lang.String methods and nothing else — an ignored `Stream.map`, an ignored `Optional.filter`, an ignored `Instant.plus`, or any project method annotated `@CheckReturnValue` is out of its reach and depends entirely on Error Prone or SpotBugs. Error Prone's ReturnValueIgnored covers a curated set of known-pure JDK and Guava methods, not arbitrary user code, so a project wanting full coverage must annotate its own APIs with `@CheckReturnValue`. Java-only paths: detekt's IgnoredReturnValue requires type resolution to be useful on Kotlin. The near-miss is the trap for a line-anchored pattern: `String slug = name.trim().toLowerCase()...` starts with a type and an assignment, and `audit.append(slug)` is a genuinely mutating builder call.

evidence.source: errorprone.info bug patterns — ReturnValueIgnored (ERROR), CheckReturnValue (ERROR); spotbugs.readthedocs.io bug descriptions — RV_RETURN_VALUE_IGNORED, 'Method ignores return value'; detekt.dev potential-bugs (IgnoredReturnValue).

classes.title: Closeable opened outside try-with-resources
agentModes: Opens a stream, reader or socket in a plain assignment because try-with-resources would have restructured the method it was editing
Moves a resource out of its try-with-resources header while extracting a variable, and does not add a close
Adds a second resource to an existing method by copying the assignment form rather than the try header
classes.gapNotes: Heuristic on two counts. It recognises a closed list of JDK constructors, so a project-specific Closeable, a factory method (`Files.newInputStream`, `HttpClient.newHttpClient`), or a resource obtained from a builder is missed entirely — PMD's CloseResource is the only detector that generalises, and it needs its `types`/`closeTargets` properties extended to know about project types. It leans on line-anchoring to distinguish an assignment from a try-with-resources header, which fails the moment the header wraps across lines. It also cannot see a resource correctly closed in a `finally` block and will flag it. Kotlin's `use { }` idiom is not modelled at all; detekt's MissingUseCall exists but is not claimed here because it was not confirmed against a specific Kotlin fixture shape in this research pass.

evidence.source: docs.pmd-code.org PMD 7 java errorprone (CloseResource); Java language specification try-with-resources.

classes.title: Thread.sleep standing in for a real wait condition in a test
agentModes: Adds Thread.sleep to make an intermittently failing async test pass on the machine it is running on
Increases an existing sleep when the test fails again, rather than waiting on the condition
Uses a sleep because it does not know which awaiting primitive the project already has
classes.gapNotes: The call site is matched exactly, but whether that call is a defect is not decidable from the text. Regex-only: no linter in this ecosystem ships a rule banning Thread.sleep in tests, and no honest one could — a sleep is correct when the test is deliberately exercising timing. That makes this a project-policy class whose value comes from the ledger, not the match. It does not see the same mistake expressed through Awaitility with a fixed `pollDelay`, a busy-wait loop, or a Kotlin `runBlocking { delay(500) }` — `delay(` was deliberately left out of the pattern because it collides with too many legitimate project method names. The near-miss carries the two traps: `drained.await(5, TimeUnit.SECONDS)` is a real condition wait using the same TimeUnit import, and a method named `reportsSleepBudget` mentions sleep without calling it.

evidence.source: java.lang.Thread.sleep and java.util.concurrent.TimeUnit.sleep are JDK APIs; the judgement that their use in a test is a synchronisation smell is jig's policy, backed by no tool rule id — hence the missing tool-rule detector.

classes.title: equals overridden without hashCode (or the reverse)
agentModes: Writes equals to make a test comparison pass and stops there, silently breaking every HashMap and HashSet holding the type
Regenerates equals after adding a field but leaves hashCode covering the old field set
Adds equals to a class it converted from a record, losing the record's generated hashCode
classes.gapNotes: Tool-rule only, because the mistake is the absence of a method: a regex can see `equals` present but cannot prove `hashCode` missing from the same class without parsing class bodies, and a file with two classes defeats any whole-file proximity heuristic. None of these rules catches the worse variant that IS present in both methods — a hashCode that covers fewer fields than equals, which satisfies every rule here and still breaks hash lookups. Nor do they catch equals overloaded on the concrete type (`boolean equals(Sku other)`) instead of overridden on Object; Error Prone has bug patterns in that area but none was confirmed by name in this research pass, so none is claimed.

evidence.source: checkstyle.org coding category (EqualsHashCode); docs.pmd-code.org PMD 7 java errorprone (OverrideBothEqualsAndHashcode); detekt.dev potential-bugs ruleset (EqualsWithHashCodeExist).
